name: Hacker's Diet

image.caption: Tracking with the Hacker Diet - Jodi Schneider

lead: The Hacker's Diet is a free book and set of tools by Autodesk founder John Walker that treats weight loss as a control problem: record what you eat and weigh, smooth the daily noise, and adjust intake or exercise to move the trend line. Leaner body fat is the appearance payoff, with the logging habit as the mechanism.

It began as an electronic book in 1991 and has been republished on the web, as an e-book and with spreadsheets and an online tracker. Walker reports going from 98 kg to 66 kg in a year; the wider evidence is the general literature on self-monitoring in weight management rather than trials of this book specifically.

paras: Practitioners log a daily weight, compute an exponentially smoothed trend that filters out water-weight swings, and compare it with calorie intake and exercise logs. Tools include Walker's spreadsheets, an online log, a Palm app (Eat Watch) and paper charts. Readers on Hacker News describe it as a popular reference for numerically minded dieters.

It is a calorie-tracking approach with no drugs or procedures. People who find tracking stressful, or who have a history of disordered eating, may find numerical logging unhelpful; individuals with medical conditions are usually advised to consult a clinician about weight-loss targets.

angle.text: The method is a structured way of tracking and managing calorie balance. Followers use the trend line to lose fat steadily and then to watch for regain.

lead: The Hacker's Diet is a weight-management guide by John Walker, founder of Autodesk, that frames dieting as an engineering and feedback problem. It was first written in 1991 as an electronic book.[1]

People use it to lose fat and so change their physique and facial leanness. The method models the body as a system whose weight depends on the gap between calories eaten and calories burned; the dieter records weight and intake, uses exponential moving averages to smooth water fluctuations, and uses trend lines to catch regain early.[1]

The book has been available free on Walker's Fourmilab site in successive editions: web editions in the 1990s, a standards-compliant fourth edition in November 2005 and an EPUB in 2011, along with spreadsheets and an online tool.[2] It has been repeatedly discussed on Hacker News since 2009.[3][3]

paras: Walker describes the body as a rubber bag whose weight depends on calorie input and output. Dieters track intake and weight, then raise or lower food or exercise accordingly. Smoothing the noisy daily weight yields a trend, and the trend gives early warning of regain after a goal is reached.[1]
Supporting tools include Excel spreadsheets, a free web application for weights, exercise and charts, a Palm-based nutrition and exercise log, and paper-and-pencil alternatives.[2]

The book originated as an electronic book in 1991.[1] Fourmilab lists a 1994 third edition, a November 2005 fourth edition that is content-identical but reformatted, and an EPUB edition from 2011.[2] Walker reports losing from 98 kg to 66 kg in a year and keeping the weight stable afterward.[1]
The Hacker News community has discussed the book in threads in 2009, 2015, 2018 and 2022, with commenters sharing their own tracking setups.[3][3][3][3][3][3]
